questions.topicName: Histology of the Respiratory Tract
questions.stem: This midsagittal diagram of the head and neck labels the epiglottis at the entrance to the larynx. What is its primary function?

choices.label: E
choices.text: Covering the laryngeal opening during swallowing

explanation.summary: During swallowing the epiglottis folds back over the laryngeal inlet, directing food into the esophagus and protecting the airway from aspiration.
explanation.whyCorrect: During swallowing the epiglottis folds back over the laryngeal inlet, directing food into the esophagus and protecting the airway from aspiration.

questions.topicName: Histology of the Respiratory Tract
questions.stem: This cadaveric midsagittal section of the head is used to highlight the olfactory epithelium. Which region of the respiratory tract is being displayed?

explanation.summary: The section shows the nasal septum and conchae of the nasal cavity, where the olfactory epithelium sits in the roof.
explanation.whyCorrect: The section shows the nasal septum and conchae of the nasal cavity, where the olfactory epithelium sits in the roof.

questions.imageRef: repic-057_Brick Exchange - Histology of the Respiratory Tract_p5_1.png

questions.topicName: Histology of the Respiratory Tract
questions.stem: This airway wall shows a mucosa of tall pseudostratified ciliated columnar epithelium, a submucosa, and an underlying plate of pale hyaline cartilage with chondrocytes in lacunae. Which structure is this section most consistent with?

explanation.summary: Pseudostratified ciliated columnar (respiratory) epithelium resting on a mucosa/submucosa supported by hyaline cartilage is characteristic of the trachea and large bronchi of the conducting airways.
explanation.whyCorrect: Pseudostratified ciliated columnar (respiratory) epithelium resting on a mucosa/submucosa supported by hyaline cartilage is characteristic of the trachea and large bronchi of the conducting airways.

questions.imageRef: repic-138_Brick Exchange - Histology of the Respiratory Tract_p13_1.png

questions.topicName: Histology of the Respiratory Tract
questions.stem: A small airway with folded epithelium is encircled by a layer of smooth muscle and surrounded by thin-walled air spaces (alveoli), with no cartilage present. What airway is shown?

explanation.summary: A small conducting airway lacking cartilage and glands but wrapped by a relatively prominent smooth muscle layer, surrounded by alveoli, identifies a bronchiole; the absence of cartilage distinguishes it from bronchi.
explanation.whyCorrect: A small conducting airway lacking cartilage and glands but wrapped by a relatively prominent smooth muscle layer, surrounded by alveoli, identifies a bronchiole; the absence of cartilage distinguishes it from bronchi.

questions.imageRef: repic-139_Brick Exchange - Histology of the Respiratory Tract_p15_1.png

questions.topicName: Histology of the Respiratory Tract
questions.stem: This lung section (40X) shows a large conducting airway lined by pseudostratified ciliated columnar epithelium. What is the primary function of this epithelial lining?

explanation.summary: The bronchial epithelium is pseudostratified ciliated columnar with goblet cells; cilia sweep mucus-trapped debris up toward the pharynx (mucociliary escalator). Gas exchange occurs only in alveoli, not conducting airways.
explanation.whyCorrect: The bronchial epithelium is pseudostratified ciliated columnar with goblet cells; cilia sweep mucus-trapped debris up toward the pharynx (mucociliary escalator). Gas exchange occurs only in alveoli, not conducting airways.

questions.imageRef: repic-140_Brick Exchange - Histology of the Respiratory Tract_p16_1.png

questions.topicName: Histology of the Respiratory Tract
questions.stem: This lung histology is labeled with a respiratory bronchiole (RB), alveolar ducts (AD), alveolar sacs (AS), and alveoli (A). Which functional zone of the respiratory system does this region represent?

choices.label: E
choices.text: The bronchial tree proximal to terminal bronchioles

explanation.summary: Respiratory bronchioles, alveolar ducts, sacs, and alveoli make up the respiratory zone where gas exchange occurs, distinguishing it from the purely conducting airways.
explanation.whyCorrect: Respiratory bronchioles, alveolar ducts, sacs, and alveoli make up the respiratory zone where gas exchange occurs, distinguishing it from the purely conducting airways.

questions.imageRef: repic-141_Brick Exchange - Histology of the Respiratory Tract_p17_1.png

questions.topicName: Histology of the Respiratory Tract
questions.stem: In this diagram of an alveolus, what is the principal function of the Type 2 pneumocyte?

choices.label: B
choices.text: Forming the thin barrier for gas diffusion

choices.label: E
choices.text: Conducting air toward the alveolar duct

explanation.summary: Type 2 pneumocytes (cuboidal cells) secrete surfactant, which reduces surface tension and prevents alveolar collapse. Type 1 pneumocytes form the thin gas-exchange surface, and dust cells (macrophages) clear debris.
explanation.whyCorrect: Type 2 pneumocytes (cuboidal cells) secrete surfactant, which reduces surface tension and prevents alveolar collapse. Type 1 pneumocytes form the thin gas-exchange surface, and dust cells (macrophages) clear debris.

questions.imageRef: repic-142_Brick Exchange - Histology of the Respiratory Tract_p18_1.png

questions.topicName: Histology of the Respiratory Tract
questions.stem: This H&E section shows thin-walled air spaces lined by Type 1 and Type 2 pneumocytes with an alveolar macrophage. From which organ is this tissue taken?

explanation.summary: The delicate alveolar architecture with Type 1/Type 2 pneumocytes and macrophages is characteristic of lung parenchyma.
explanation.whyCorrect: The delicate alveolar architecture with Type 1/Type 2 pneumocytes and macrophages is characteristic of lung parenchyma.

questions.imageRef: repic-143_Brick Exchange - Histology of the Respiratory Tract_p21_1.png

questions.topicName: Histology of the Respiratory Tract
questions.stem: At the edge of this lung section a thin fibrous membrane (bracketed) covers the alveolar tissue. What is the functional role of this membrane?

explanation.summary: The visceral pleura is a serous membrane covering the lung; together with the parietal pleura and pleural fluid it minimizes friction as the lung expands and recoils during breathing.
explanation.whyCorrect: The visceral pleura is a serous membrane covering the lung; together with the parietal pleura and pleural fluid it minimizes friction as the lung expands and recoils during breathing.

questions.imageRef: repic-144_Brick Exchange - Histology of the Respiratory Tract_p22_1.png

questions.topicName: Histology of the Respiratory Tract
questions.stem: This high-power view shows the epithelium that lines the trachea, with an apical row of cilia and a basal lamina propria. What is its main functional role?

choices.label: C
choices.text: Moving a mucus layer with trapped particles

explanation.summary: Pseudostratified ciliated columnar epithelium with goblet cells lines the trachea; coordinated ciliary beating propels mucus and trapped debris upward (mucociliary escalator).
explanation.whyCorrect: Pseudostratified ciliated columnar epithelium with goblet cells lines the trachea; coordinated ciliary beating propels mucus and trapped debris upward (mucociliary escalator).

questions.imageRef: repic-145_Brick Exchange - Histology of the Respiratory Tract_p3_1.png

questions.topicName: Histology of the Respiratory Tract
questions.stem: This specialized pseudostratified epithelium in the roof of the nasal cavity contains bipolar sensory neurons (ON) among supporting (S) and basal (B) cells. What special sense does it mediate?

explanation.summary: The olfactory epithelium contains bipolar olfactory receptor neurons whose cilia detect odorants; supporting (sustentacular) and basal cells complete the epithelium.
explanation.whyCorrect: The olfactory epithelium contains bipolar olfactory receptor neurons whose cilia detect odorants; supporting (sustentacular) and basal cells complete the epithelium.

questions.imageRef: repic-146_Brick Exchange - Histology of the Respiratory Tract_p6_1.png

questions.topicName: Histology of the Respiratory Tract
questions.stem: This diagram maps epithelial types onto the upper airway, showing stratified squamous epithelium in the oropharynx rather than ciliated epithelium. Why is stratified squamous epithelium found there?

choices.label: C
choices.text: To absorb nutrients from swallowed food

choices.label: D
choices.text: To improve ciliary clearance of particles

choices.label: E
choices.text: To maximize gas exchange with blood

explanation.summary: The oropharynx is a shared food and air passage; stratified squamous epithelium resists the abrasion of food boluses, unlike the delicate ciliated epithelium of purely respiratory passages.
explanation.whyCorrect: The oropharynx is a shared food and air passage; stratified squamous epithelium resists the abrasion of food boluses, unlike the delicate ciliated epithelium of purely respiratory passages.

questions.imageRef: repic-147_Brick Exchange - Histology of the Respiratory Tract_p7_1.png

questions.topicName: Histology of the Respiratory Tract
questions.stem: This respiratory epithelium contains ciliated columnar cells, basal cells, and goblet cells. What is the role of the goblet cells?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Beating rhythmically to propel the mucus layer

choices.label: B
choices.text: Secreting mucus that traps inhaled particles

choices.label: C
choices.text: Carrying out gas exchange with capillaries

choices.label: D
choices.text: Serving as stem cells to regenerate the epithelium

explanation.summary: Goblet cells secrete mucus that traps debris and microbes; the cilia of columnar cells then sweep this mucus toward the pharynx, while basal cells act as the regenerative reserve.
explanation.whyCorrect: Goblet cells secrete mucus that traps debris and microbes; the cilia of columnar cells then sweep this mucus toward the pharynx, while basal cells act as the regenerative reserve.

questions.imageRef: repic-148_Brick Exchange - Histology of the Respiratory Tract_p8_1.png

questions.topicName: Histology of the Respiratory Tract
questions.stem: This nonkeratinizing stratified epithelium overlying a lamina propria lines a region shared by the digestive and respiratory tracts. Which region is it most likely from?

explanation.summary: Nonkeratinizing stratified squamous epithelium lines areas subject to abrasion such as the oropharynx and laryngopharynx, protecting against the passage of food.
explanation.whyCorrect: Nonkeratinizing stratified squamous epithelium lines areas subject to abrasion such as the oropharynx and laryngopharynx, protecting against the passage of food.

questions.imageRef: repic-149_Brick Exchange - Histology of the Respiratory Tract_p9_1.png

questions.topicName: Histology of the Respiratory Tract
questions.stem: This diagram shows O2 and CO2 crossing the structure between alveolar air and blood. By what mechanism do these gases cross this barrier?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Secondary active transport coupled to sodium

choices.label: D
choices.text: Osmosis of dissolved gas with water

explanation.summary: Gas exchange across the blood-air barrier is passive: O2 and CO2 diffuse down their respective partial pressure gradients through the thin Type 1 pneumocyte, fused basement membrane, and capillary endothelium.
explanation.whyCorrect: Gas exchange across the blood-air barrier is passive: O2 and CO2 diffuse down their respective partial pressure gradients through the thin Type 1 pneumocyte, fused basement membrane, and capillary endothelium.

questions.imageRef: repic-749_Brick Exchange - Histology of the Respiratory Tract_p19_1.png

questions.topicName: Development of the Respiratory Tract
questions.stem: This cross-section shows a thin-walled air sac with squamous lining cells, a scattered wandering phagocyte, a cuboidal cell secreting a thin film into the airspace, and a surrounding capillary containing red cells. Which cell type here is responsible for reducing surface tension and preventing collapse of this structure?

explanation.summary: The cuboidal type II pneumocyte secretes pulmonary surfactant, which lowers alveolar surface tension and prevents alveolar collapse at end-expiration. Type I pneumocytes form the thin gas-exchange surface, and macrophages clear debris; endothelial cells line the capillary.
explanation.whyCorrect: The cuboidal type II pneumocyte secretes pulmonary surfactant, which lowers alveolar surface tension and prevents alveolar collapse at end-expiration. Type I pneumocytes form the thin gas-exchange surface, and macrophages clear debris; endothelial cells line the capillary.

questions.imageRef: repic-108_Brick Exchange - Development of the Respiratory Tract_p10_1.png

questions.topicName: Development of the Respiratory Tract
questions.stem: This H&E-stained section shows thin-walled air sacs opening off a larger conducting passage. From which organ is this tissue taken?

explanation.summary: The delicate polygonal air spaces (alveoli) with thin capillary-containing septa opening off a bronchiolar lumen are the defining histologic architecture of lung parenchyma, specialized for gas exchange.
explanation.whyCorrect: The delicate polygonal air spaces (alveoli) with thin capillary-containing septa opening off a bronchiolar lumen are the defining histologic architecture of lung parenchyma, specialized for gas exchange.

questions.imageRef: repic-109_Brick Exchange - Development of the Respiratory Tract_p12_1.png

questions.topicName: Development of the Respiratory Tract
questions.stem: In this magnified developing lung, the airway is still lined by tall cuboidal cells with only sparse nearby capillaries. Which stage of lung development does this represent?

choices.label: E
choices.text: Terminal air sac stage with surfactant

explanation.summary: A thick cuboidal epithelium separated from capillaries by abundant mesoderm indicates an immature stage with a thick air-blood barrier; the epithelium has not yet thinned into type 1 pneumocytes needed for efficient gas exchange.
explanation.whyCorrect: A thick cuboidal epithelium separated from capillaries by abundant mesoderm indicates an immature stage with a thick air-blood barrier; the epithelium has not yet thinned into type 1 pneumocytes needed for efficient gas exchange.

questions.imageRef: repic-110_Brick Exchange - Development of the Respiratory Tract_p7_1.png

questions.topicName: Development of the Respiratory Tract
questions.stem: This magnified alveolar wall shows flat cells lining most of the surface and scattered rounded granular cells at the corners, adjacent to capillaries. What is the key function of the rounded granular cell type shown?

choices.label: C
choices.text: Formation of the thin gas-diffusion surface

choices.label: E
choices.text: Conduction of air to the alveoli

explanation.summary: The cuboidal granular cells are type 2 pneumocytes, which secrete surfactant that lowers surface tension and prevents alveolar collapse; the flat cells are type 1 pneumocytes forming the diffusion barrier.
explanation.whyCorrect: The cuboidal granular cells are type 2 pneumocytes, which secrete surfactant that lowers surface tension and prevents alveolar collapse; the flat cells are type 1 pneumocytes forming the diffusion barrier.

questions.imageRef: repic-111_Brick Exchange - Development of the Respiratory Tract_p8_1.png

questions.topicName: Development of the Respiratory Tract
questions.stem: This timeline maps lung development onto gestational weeks. At approximately which point does the lung first become capable of supporting respiration (gas exchange)?

explanation.summary: Respiration becomes possible near the canalicular-to-saccular transition (~24-26 weeks) once a thin air-blood barrier forms and type 2 pneumocytes begin surfactant production, which is why this marks the threshold of viability for premature infants.
explanation.whyCorrect: Respiration becomes possible near the canalicular-to-saccular transition (~24-26 weeks) once a thin air-blood barrier forms and type 2 pneumocytes begin surfactant production, which is why this marks the threshold of viability for premature infants.

questions.imageRef: repic-715_Brick Exchange - Development of the Respiratory Tract_p15_1.png

questions.topicName: Development of the Respiratory Tract
questions.stem: This sequence shows the foregut giving rise to a ventral outgrowth that is progressively partitioned. What process is being illustrated?

choices.label: B
choices.text: Formation of the diaphragm from the septum transversum

choices.label: C
choices.text: Fusion of the pleural and pericardial cavities

choices.label: D
choices.text: Rotation of the primitive heart tube

choices.label: E
choices.text: Separation of the trachea from the esophagus

explanation.summary: The respiratory diverticulum buds from the ventral foregut and is separated from the future esophagus by tracheoesophageal ridges that fuse into a septum; failure of this process produces tracheoesophageal fistula.
explanation.whyCorrect: The respiratory diverticulum buds from the ventral foregut and is separated from the future esophagus by tracheoesophageal ridges that fuse into a septum; failure of this process produces tracheoesophageal fistula.

questions.imageRef: repic-716_Brick Exchange - Development of the Respiratory Tract_p3_1.png

questions.topicName: Development of the Respiratory Tract
questions.stem: From 28 to 56 days, the paired outgrowths shown undergo repeated dichotomous division into progressively smaller branches. What does this branching establish?

choices.label: B
choices.text: The conducting airway tree and lung lobes

choices.label: D
choices.text: The pulmonary venous return to the left atrium

explanation.summary: Sequential division of secondary and tertiary bronchial buds during the pseudoglandular period lays down the branching conducting airways and defines the lobar pattern (three lobes on the right, two on the left).
explanation.whyCorrect: Sequential division of secondary and tertiary bronchial buds during the pseudoglandular period lays down the branching conducting airways and defines the lobar pattern (three lobes on the right, two on the left).

questions.topicName: Anatomy of the Upper Respiratory Tract
questions.stem: This diagram shows the great vessels of the neck. Why does the right common carotid artery arise differently from the left?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Both arise directly from the ascending aorta before the arch

choices.label: B
choices.text: The right arises from the brachiocephalic trunk, whereas the left branches directly off the aortic arch

choices.label: C
choices.text: The right arises from the subclavian and the left from the pulmonary trunk

choices.label: D
choices.text: The right arises from the aortic arch and the left from the vertebral artery

choices.label: E
choices.text: Both arise from the brachiocephalic trunk but on opposite sides

explanation.summary: The aortic arch gives off the brachiocephalic trunk, left common carotid, and left subclavian. The brachiocephalic trunk then splits into the right common carotid and right subclavian, so only the right common carotid is a second-order branch.
explanation.whyCorrect: The aortic arch gives off the brachiocephalic trunk, left common carotid, and left subclavian. The brachiocephalic trunk then splits into the right common carotid and right subclavian, so only the right common carotid is a second-order branch.

questions.imageRef: repic-023_Brick Exchange - Anatomy of the Upper Respiratory Tract_p11_1.png

questions.topicName: Anatomy of the Upper Respiratory Tract
questions.stem: This figure shows the arterial anastomoses of the nasal septum, including the anterior plexus outlined at the front. What common clinical event is this anterior region most associated with?

choices.label: E
choices.text: Loss of the sense of smell

explanation.summary: The anterior septal anastomosis (Kiesselbach plexus) is a superficial convergence of several arteries and is the site of roughly 90% of nosebleeds. The posterior Woodruff plexus accounts for less common but heavier posterior bleeds.
explanation.whyCorrect: The anterior septal anastomosis (Kiesselbach plexus) is a superficial convergence of several arteries and is the site of roughly 90% of nosebleeds. The posterior Woodruff plexus accounts for less common but heavier posterior bleeds.

questions.imageRef: repic-024_Brick Exchange - Anatomy of the Upper Respiratory Tract_p12_1.png

questions.topicName: Anatomy of the Upper Respiratory Tract
questions.stem: The paranasal sinuses are shown draining into the nasal cavity. Which of these sinuses is the largest and most frequently involved in sinusitis?

explanation.summary: The maxillary sinuses are the largest paranasal sinuses. Because their ostium sits high on the medial wall, gravity-dependent drainage is poor, making them the most commonly infected sinus.
explanation.whyCorrect: The maxillary sinuses are the largest paranasal sinuses. Because their ostium sits high on the medial wall, gravity-dependent drainage is poor, making them the most commonly infected sinus.

questions.imageRef: repic-025_Brick Exchange - Anatomy of the Upper Respiratory Tract_p14_1.png

questions.topicName: Anatomy of the Upper Respiratory Tract
questions.stem: This sagittal view color-codes the three pharyngeal regions. Which region receives the opening of the pharyngotympanic (auditory) tube?

explanation.summary: The pharyngotympanic (Eustachian) tube opens into the nasopharynx, equalizing middle-ear pressure. The oropharynx lies behind the mouth and the laryngopharynx opens into the larynx and esophagus.
explanation.whyCorrect: The pharyngotympanic (Eustachian) tube opens into the nasopharynx, equalizing middle-ear pressure. The oropharynx lies behind the mouth and the laryngopharynx opens into the larynx and esophagus.

questions.imageRef: repic-026_Brick Exchange - Anatomy of the Upper Respiratory Tract_p17_1.png

questions.topicName: Anatomy of the Upper Respiratory Tract
questions.stem: This posterior view shows nerves converging on the pharyngeal muscles. Which nerve provides most of the motor innervation to the pharyngeal constrictors via the pharyngeal plexus?

explanation.summary: The pharyngeal plexus carries motor fibers from the vagus (CN X) to all pharyngeal constrictors except stylopharyngeus (CN IX). CN IX contributes mainly sensory fibers to the plexus.
explanation.whyCorrect: The pharyngeal plexus carries motor fibers from the vagus (CN X) to all pharyngeal constrictors except stylopharyngeus (CN IX). CN IX contributes mainly sensory fibers to the plexus.

questions.imageRef: repic-027_Brick Exchange - Anatomy of the Upper Respiratory Tract_p22_1.png

questions.topicName: Anatomy of the Upper Respiratory Tract
questions.stem: In this open-mouth view, the paired masses seen on either side of the throat (between the palatine arches) are lymphoid tissue. What is their immunological role?

choices.label: A
choices.text: They are cartilage plates that keep the pharynx open

choices.label: B
choices.text: They are taste-bud clusters that detect bitter compounds

choices.label: C
choices.text: They are palatine tonsils that sample antigens

choices.label: D
choices.text: They are muscles that close the airway during swallowing

choices.label: E
choices.text: They are salivary glands that secrete digestive enzymes

explanation.summary: The palatine tonsils are aggregates of mucosa-associated lymphoid tissue forming part of Waldeyer's ring. They trap pathogens entering via the mouth and nose and mount local immune responses.
explanation.whyCorrect: The palatine tonsils are aggregates of mucosa-associated lymphoid tissue forming part of Waldeyer's ring. They trap pathogens entering via the mouth and nose and mount local immune responses.

questions.imageRef: repic-028_Brick Exchange - Anatomy of the Upper Respiratory Tract_p24_1.png

questions.topicName: Anatomy of the Upper Respiratory Tract
questions.stem: This diagram shows the arterial supply to the pharynx and palatine tonsil. Which vessel is the principal source of significant hemorrhage during a tonsillectomy?

choices.label: B
choices.text: Tonsillar branch of the facial artery

explanation.summary: The palatine tonsil is chiefly supplied by the tonsillar branch of the facial artery, which is the main vessel responsible for post-tonsillectomy bleeding. The internal carotid gives no branches in the neck, and the other named external carotid branches supply the tonsil only minimally.
explanation.whyCorrect: The palatine tonsil is chiefly supplied by the tonsillar branch of the facial artery, which is the main vessel responsible for post-tonsillectomy bleeding. The internal carotid gives no branches in the neck, and the other named external carotid branches supply the tonsil only minimally.

questions.imageRef: repic-029_Brick Exchange - Anatomy of the Upper Respiratory Tract_p25_1.png

questions.topicName: Anatomy of the Upper Respiratory Tract
questions.stem: This posterior view shows the laryngopharynx. The deep recess lateral to the laryngeal inlet is clinically important primarily because it is a common site for what?

choices.label: B
choices.text: Origin of the recurrent laryngeal nerve

explanation.summary: The piriform fossa is a frequent site for lodged foreign bodies (e.g., fish bones); its mucosa also overlies the internal laryngeal nerve, which can be injured during foreign-body removal.
explanation.whyCorrect: The piriform fossa is a frequent site for lodged foreign bodies (e.g., fish bones); its mucosa also overlies the internal laryngeal nerve, which can be injured during foreign-body removal.

questions.imageRef: repic-030_Brick Exchange - Anatomy of the Upper Respiratory Tract_p27_1.png

questions.topicName: Anatomy of the Upper Respiratory Tract
questions.stem: This midsagittal section divides the pharynx into three color-coded regions. Which region contains the openings of the pharyngotympanic (auditory) tubes?

explanation.summary: The auditory (Eustachian) tubes open into the lateral walls of the nasopharynx, allowing middle-ear pressure equalization; this explains why nasopharyngeal pathology can cause conductive hearing problems.
explanation.whyCorrect: The auditory (Eustachian) tubes open into the lateral walls of the nasopharynx, allowing middle-ear pressure equalization; this explains why nasopharyngeal pathology can cause conductive hearing problems.

questions.topicName: Anatomy of the Upper Respiratory Tract
questions.stem: In this anterior view of the laryngeal skeleton, the membrane bridging the two lower cartilages is the site incised during which emergency airway procedure?

choices.label: C
choices.text: Tracheostomy at the second tracheal ring

explanation.summary: The cricothyroid membrane, lying between the thyroid and cricoid cartilages, is the landmark for an emergency cricothyroidotomy because it is superficial, relatively avascular, and easily palpable.
explanation.whyCorrect: The cricothyroid membrane, lying between the thyroid and cricoid cartilages, is the landmark for an emergency cricothyroidotomy because it is superficial, relatively avascular, and easily palpable.

questions.imageRef: repic-032_Brick Exchange - Anatomy of the Upper Respiratory Tract_p31_1.png

questions.topicName: Anatomy of the Upper Respiratory Tract
questions.stem: This endoscopic photograph shows the laryngeal inlet during laryngoscopy. The paired mobile structures at the posterior ends of the vocal cords are functionally important because they do what?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Rotate to abduct and adduct the vocal cords

choices.label: B
choices.text: Filter particulate matter from inspired air

choices.label: D
choices.text: Anchor the epiglottis to the hyoid bone

explanation.summary: The arytenoid cartilages articulate with the cricoid and are moved by the intrinsic laryngeal muscles; their rotation and gliding open and close the rima glottidis, controlling airflow and phonation.
explanation.whyCorrect: The arytenoid cartilages articulate with the cricoid and are moved by the intrinsic laryngeal muscles; their rotation and gliding open and close the rima glottidis, controlling airflow and phonation.

questions.imageRef: repic-033_Brick Exchange - Anatomy of the Upper Respiratory Tract_p33_1.png

questions.topicName: Anatomy of the Upper Respiratory Tract
questions.stem: This sagittal figure shows the structures forming the nasal septum. The bony part of the septum is formed principally by which two bones?

choices.label: E
choices.text: Perpendicular plate of the ethmoid and the vomer

explanation.summary: The bony nasal septum is formed superiorly by the perpendicular plate of the ethmoid and inferiorly/posteriorly by the vomer, with the septal cartilage completing the septum anteriorly.
explanation.whyCorrect: The bony nasal septum is formed superiorly by the perpendicular plate of the ethmoid and inferiorly/posteriorly by the vomer, with the septal cartilage completing the septum anteriorly.

questions.imageRef: repic-034_Brick Exchange - Anatomy of the Upper Respiratory Tract_p6_1.png

questions.topicName: Anatomy of the Upper Respiratory Tract
questions.stem: This coronal section through the facial skeleton shows several air-filled, mucosa-lined cavities embedded within the frontal, ethmoid, sphenoid, and maxillary bones. What is the primary functional role of these paired cavities?

choices.label: A
choices.text: They lighten the skull and help warm and humidify inspired air

choices.label: B
choices.text: They provide the bony attachment for the extraocular muscles

choices.label: C
choices.text: They produce and secrete tears that drain to the eye

choices.label: D
choices.text: They house the primary olfactory receptor neurons

choices.label: E
choices.text: They generate cerebrospinal fluid for the anterior cranial fossa

explanation.summary: The cavities shown are the paranasal sinuses (frontal, ethmoid, sphenoid, maxillary). They reduce skull weight, add resonance to the voice, and their mucosa helps condition (warm/humidify) inspired air. Olfaction occurs at the cribriform plate, and tear production is a lacrimal-gland function.
explanation.whyCorrect: The cavities shown are the paranasal sinuses (frontal, ethmoid, sphenoid, maxillary). They reduce skull weight, add resonance to the voice, and their mucosa helps condition (warm/humidify) inspired air. Olfaction occurs at the cribriform plate, and tear production is a lacrimal-gland function.

questions.imageRef: repic-035_Brick Exchange - Anatomy of the Upper Respiratory Tract_p7_1.png

questions.topicName: Anatomy of the Upper Respiratory Tract
questions.stem: This coronal view of the nasal cavity highlights three paired, scroll-like bony projections along the lateral wall (color-coded) with air passages beneath each. What is the chief physiologic purpose of these projections?

choices.label: A
choices.text: They anchor the vocal cords during phonation

choices.label: B
choices.text: They serve as the primary site of gas exchange

choices.label: C
choices.text: They contain the sensory endings for the gag reflex

choices.label: D
choices.text: They form the bony support of the hard palate

choices.label: E
choices.text: They increase mucosal surface area to warm, humidify, and filter inspired air

explanation.summary: The projections are the nasal conchae (turbinates). By creating turbulent airflow over a large mucosal surface, they warm, humidify, and filter inspired air. The spaces beneath them are the meatuses, into which sinuses and the nasolacrimal duct drain.
explanation.whyCorrect: The projections are the nasal conchae (turbinates). By creating turbulent airflow over a large mucosal surface, they warm, humidify, and filter inspired air. The spaces beneath them are the meatuses, into which sinuses and the nasolacrimal duct drain.

questions.imageRef: repic-036_Brick Exchange - Anatomy of the Upper Respiratory Tract_p8_1.png

questions.topicName: Anatomy of the Upper Respiratory Tract
questions.stem: This sagittal view of the lateral nasal wall shows the openings of the paranasal sinuses and the nasolacrimal duct into the nasal passages. What clinical phenomenon is explained by the drainage pathway of the nasolacrimal duct shown here?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Loss of smell when the frontal sinus is blocked

choices.label: D
choices.text: Hoarseness caused by postnasal drip onto the vocal cords

choices.label: E
choices.text: Nosebleeds arising from the sphenoid sinus

explanation.summary: The nasolacrimal duct drains lacrimal fluid from the medial canthus of the eye into the inferior meatus of the nasal cavity. This is why excess tears (crying) produce a runny nose. Most paranasal sinuses drain into the middle meatus.

questions.stem: The airways from the trachea through the terminal bronchioles are grouped as the 'conducting zone.' What physiological property defines this zone?

choices.text: It is the primary site of oxygen–carbon dioxide exchange

choices.label: B
choices.text: It is lined entirely by gas-exchanging alveoli

explanation.summary: The diaphragm performs most of the work of quiet inspiration; its contraction flattens the dome, increasing thoracic volume. The scalenes and external intercostals assist, while sternocleidomastoid and other accessory muscles are recruited only in forced inspiration. Abdominal muscles and internal intercostals drive forced expiration.

choices.label: C

choices.label: D

choices.label: E

explanation.summary: The costodiaphragmatic recess is the deep pleural gutter between the costal and diaphragmatic pleura that lung tissue only fills during deep inspiration. questions.stem: This figure separates the muscles of inspiration from the muscles of expiration. During QUIET (resting) breathing, expiration is accomplished mainly by which mechanism?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Passive elastic recoil of the lungs and chest wall

choices.label: B
choices.text: Contraction of the diaphragm pushing air out

choices.label: C
choices.text: Forceful contraction of the internal intercostals

choices.label: D
choices.text: Contraction of the scalenes and sternocleidomastoid

choices.label: E
choices.text: Contraction of the rectus abdominis and external obliques

explanation.summary: Quiet expiration is passive: the inspiratory muscles relax and the stored elastic recoil of the lungs and chest wall drives air out. The abdominal muscles and internal intercostals shown here are recruited only for active, forced expiration such as coughing or exercise.

questions.topicName: Anatomy of the Diaphragm, Ribs, and Intercostal Muscles
questions.stem: This figure contrasts the chest and diaphragm during breathing in versus breathing out. During inspiration, how does diaphragm contraction change intrathoracic pressure and drive airflow?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It relaxes and ascends, pulling air into the lungs

choices.label: B
choices.text: It domes upward, decreasing thoracic volume and pushing air in

choices.label: C
choices.text: It flattens and descends, lowering intrapleural/alveolar pressure so air flows in

choices.label: D
choices.text: It raises alveolar pressure above atmospheric, drawing air in

choices.label: E
choices.text: It has no effect on volume; only the ribs move air

explanation.summary: When the diaphragm contracts it flattens and moves down, enlarging the thoracic cavity. By Boyle's law the increased volume lowers intrapleural and alveolar pressure below atmospheric, so air flows in. During quiet expiration the diaphragm relaxes and ascends, the lungs recoil, and air passively flows out.
explanation.whyCorrect: When the diaphragm contracts it flattens and moves down, enlarging the thoracic cavity. By Boyle's law the increased volume lowers intrapleural and alveolar pressure below atmospheric, so air flows in. During quiet expiration the diaphragm relaxes and ascends, the lungs recoil, and air passively flows out.
